GAUTENG HEALTH TROUBLES

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Having its furniture seized to settle a legal claim may be a particularly low point, but it follows on years of bankruptcy in management and administration.

Unique Selling Point:
Last week the Gauteng health department had its furniture and office equipment seized to pay for a medical negligence claim of about R6,2-million. About 400 computers, 50 printers, 400 desks, 600 chairs, 200 filing cabinets, 10 fridges, 10 microwaves and three lounge suites have gone into storage -- keep in mind the total haul may not be worth more than about half a million rand. Keep in mind that the Department itself is now responsible to pay for the storage.

Think about the replacement cost and new opportunities for graft as new tenders are issued to kit out the offices. Think of the time lost as staff reportedly sit on floors and commute to offices in Pretoria to be able to work. The seizure came after action was brought by Pretoria attorney Oloff Joubert, acting on behalf of a child who suffered brain damage when she was born at the Pholosong Hospital in December 2009.

Joubert has confidentially informed us that he intends bringing further sheriff's action because of other unsettled claims -- in the interest of the children left behind. Joubert says his sense is that medical services may have improved in recent years and there seem to be fewer cases coming in, but many of the cases now crippling the system financially date back five years and more.

He argues for a system similar to the private sector where doctors have insurance for negligence claims -- since negligence payouts are not budgeted for. (Keep in mind the national backdrop -- the South African Law Reform Commission is working on ways to stop the bleeding of the fiscus through lawsuits -- some very controversial suggestions are being put forward).

But what about outstanding debts to suppliers? In May health MEC Gwen Ramokgopa conceded that the current R40.2bn budget was inadequate to cover requirements, largely due to substantial debt burden consisting of money owed to suppliers. Outstanding payments to suppliers dating back to previous years totalled R4.2bn. Commitments to long-term contracts took up R2.95bn, while possible payments for medical negligence amounted to R3.78bn.

In 2016, the health department’s legal fees amounted to R569m, pushed up by burgeoning negligence cases since 2009. The department also reported that a total of R860m meant for hospital infrastructure had been withheld from the National Treasury pending submission and approvals of plans by the department.

Of the total budget, R23.8bn was earmarked for the wage bill and R16.3bn for goods and services, while an estimated R6bn was allocated to accruals, the MEC said. "This budget is effectively not available," Ramokgopa said, "which means we have not been able to afford services in the past years and the service providers carried the public health system at a huge cost."

The National Treasury’s fourth-quarter provincial budgets and expenditure report for the 2016-17 financial year released in April showed that provincial health departments spent 63% of their health expenditure on salaries. A meagre 4.4% of the total health expenditure went to capital expenditure.

In 2016, the DEPT owed R300 million to 509 companies (mostly small and struggling...but some also large and struggling) according to answers to the DA's questions in the Gauteng Legislature. As of the end of January 2016, owed R296 million to 509 companies.

In January 2017 the DEPT said: ​As the Gauteng Department of Health we wish to inform that we are paying all our suppliers but not full amount. This is due to prioritising payment as per demands which we cannot accede to because they are higher than what we budget for. This is compounded by the fact that the Department services other provinces and countries (which payment thereof is not consistent and sufficient). We are monitoring closely the stock management over what is available and what is needed at the facilities. This is to ensure we always have enough funds to pay suppliers. It is important indicating that Medico-Legal claims dating back 2009/10 and 2011 take bulk of the Department's budget. We wish to confirm that an amount of R11 billion has been paid to suppliers in this financial year (2016/17) and this will continue until the end of March 2017. All the outstanding amount will be settled in the new financial year.

We asked where the money is going and who benefits.


Summary:
The Gauteng Health department, with a budget of R40.2 billion a year, has paid R1.017 billion in the 18 months from January 2015 to settle 185 medical negligence claims.

But the department has more than R20 billion in claims pending against it.

This is not something that is budgeted for and these claims could cripple a department already struggling to cope with staff shortages, lack of maintenance of buildings and machines and a high volume of patients.

The department has asked the Constitutional Court change the law to allow it to pay medical negligence victims with installments or as and when they need medical attention. This request has failed before the courts in the past, but the department is making yet another last-ditch effort.

The most medical negligence claims against the department originate in babies being brain-damaged at birth and by far the majority of claims originate at Chris Hani Baragwanath, where facilities are inadequate and understaffing endemic.

Press Release:


Recently furniture and office equipment were seized from the Gauteng Health Department to settle a medical negligence claim. This may seem like a particularly low point for the department, but it follows years of mismanagement and maladministration in the province. Meanwhile, more medical negligence claims are piling up for which the department cannot legally budget. Carte Blanche asks: Is Gauteng health facing an imminent financial crisis?

Script:


SCRIPT: Gauteng Health Troubles
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: Claire Mawisa
TX date: 1 October 2017

Gauteng is the fastest growing province with over 13-million people. Its thirty five state hospitals serve at least 80% of residents and many from across borders.

LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: For the Gauteng Health Department, it’s been one crisis after another.

It’s still reeling from the high cost of the Life Esidimeni tragedy -- not only money, but a cost in lives.

LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: Pathologists were on strike for three weeks in June. In July, it emerged that the department owed the National Health Laboratory Services millions. In August, the sheriff carted away furniture and computers from head office. And last month, telephone lines were cut because Telkom had not been paid.

The department’s budget has been raised to over R40 billion this year -- just less than the City of Cape Town’s entire budget. And yet, it’s battling to pay the bills. For two years, single mom Jessie Makhoba has waited for the department to pay R18 million for her 11-year-old son Sipho, who suffered brain damage during his birth at a local hospital.

JESSIE MAKHOBA: I cannot cope, I sit and think of all the things I could be doing and I can’t now. What Sipho needs is his mother’s love, if it were up to me I would not be working but I have to.

It was outstanding payouts to the Makhobas and families like them that saw the sheriff remove furniture and more from the Department. The order was obtained by medical malpractice attorney Olof Joubert.

CLAIRE MAWISA: A lot of people want to know Olof, was it a publicity stunt to get the furniture seized or was it a legitimate way to get that money for your client?

OLOF JOUBERT, MEDICAL MALPRACTICE ATTORNEY: We have attempted and have been reasonable in all aspects. There’s a major amount of money still outstanding in which they defaulted on other matters. This was not a publicity stunt at all.

Makhoba shares a tiny RDP house with two grown daughters, and Sipho who needs constant supervision. When he was born, she needed an emergency caesarean but she was sent from one hospital to the next, made to wait for hours and was subjected to painful vacuum extraction -- all to no avail.

JESSIE MAKHOBA: Around twelve they took me to the theatre for a c-section, but by then it was too late, the baby was injured.
The court vindicated Makhoba’s claim, but the battle wasn’t over.

LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: The Health Department’s core responsibility is to take care of its patients but what must happen if they are the ones that cause the damage?

The department’s legal services chief director Thulani Mlambo says they’re not allowed to budget for negligence payouts as the law deems it wasteful expenditure.

CLAIRE MAWISA: Currently how many medical negligence claims do you have?

THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: We are sitting at over 2000 matters.

CLAIRE MAWISA: What happened when the furniture was seized?

THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: The Department has not met its obligations in terms of the court order. So that’s why the sheriff had to come, and firstly attach the furniture. And then if you fail again to pay, they remove the furniture.

Mlambo didn’t want to show us the empty floors, but claimed it was business as usual inside. DA shadow MEC for health Jack Bloom was barred from paying an oversight visit.

JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: I don’t know how the staff are managing to work without furniture. I was told they hid their laptops...so maybe they still got their cell phones. I mean you can’t go on like this.

Wits Public Health Professor Laetitia Rispel, a former health department head, has warned of systemic problems for over a decade.

PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: Insufficient planning, that would be putting it euphemistically… I think there’s been poor planning, there’s been insufficient attention paid to holding people accountable.
Bloom asked for the numbers in the provincial legislature.

JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: The problem is they start off the financial year which is in April with more than R4 billion of accruals. This is basically debts that they owe to to suppliers of the Department.

PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: By the 15th of every month, each Government department has to submit a set of financials to the provincial treasury. So it’s not a sudden problem...they would have seen it coming, you know, since the beginning of the financial year.

CLAIRE MAWISA: How did we get here?

JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: Every month for goods and services they have to pay about R600 million and they only pay out R450 million. So, every month it’s a R150 million that they’re not paying. I think the staff are doing what they can...but what do you do when you don’t have an ICU bed? Or the machinery isn’t working...so you don’t pay the suppliers, machinery is not working, a baby gets brain damaged, ends up in court and the settlement could be well over R30 million.

Carte Blanche met Thembisa Nikelo two years ago. At 3, she went to hospital for burn wounds on her hands. Drips inserted into her feet became gangrenous and she had to have a double amputation to save her life. The court awarded her just over R20 million for future medical expenses and damages. Thembisa’s mother, Celina.

CELINA NIKELO: After she got injured, I had doubts about her quality of life, but her life has changed. She’s doing well in school, she's very bright and loves school. She still needs to go for check-ups, especially for her legs; there isn’t a lot of physio, but it’s a matter of changing the prosthetics as she outgrows them.

LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: The Department says the rising number of negligence claims is harming its ability to run its hospitals and clinics. In August, it asked the Constitutional Court to change the law in these cases. The court is yet to deliver judgement.

THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: What we are saying is that a 4 year old, for instance, in respect of who the court has awarded R20 million does not necessarily need that R20 million now. So we are requesting the Constitutional Court to actually allow us some kind of a certificate that can be given to that particular person who would have been wronged, to actually go to any institution in the country so that they can get care as and when it is required.

CLAIRE MAWISA: But then what about other things that are not within the scope of the Department...schools...24 hour care?

THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: We would pay as and when that particular service is actually needed.

WIHAN JOUBERT, ATTORNEY SPECIALISING IN MEDICAL LAW: The first year or the second year the department will experience some relief, but I’m afraid it will be compounded -- payments will not be made, new applications will be brought...

Medical law attorney Wihan Joubert is studying the Constitutionality of capping and staggering pay-outs. The Health Minister tasked the South African Law Reform Commission to see how the pressure of payouts can be relieved.

WIHAN JOUBERT, ATTORNEY SPECIALISING IN MEDICAL LAW: At the time of publishing my research I couldn’t find a national procedure or guideline within which complaints by patients are handled...prospective claimants walking through my door do so as a last resort. In other words, they initiated a complaint. The complaint was acknowledged and it was promised that a… an investigation process will follow. And then sometimes, up to a year or two goes by without any feedback...I’m confident that should the hospital be in a position to properly investigate and sort out complaints, the incidences will rapidly decline.

It’s rich for the Department to plead poverty, says Morné Mostert of civil rights watchdog AfriForum. They did a private investigation into a 2015 tender for equipment at a large Gauteng hospital after receiving leaked documents.

MORNÉ MOSTERT, AFRIFORUM: Company A tendered for 24.1 million. Company B tendered for just over 12.7 million. Company B was disqualified on one single point on the tender evaluation form… All the information was on an annexure to the tender documentation and the bid acquisition committee disregarded that.

A middleman appeared to have been paid to make sure Company A, a multinational, gets the deal at double the price. Afriforum asked the police and foreign anti-corruption agencies to investigate the wasteful expenditure.

The Department did not respond to our questions about the tender.

LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: Whether corruption, or rampant negligence -- the spectre of bankruptcy is turning the screws on the Department to take action…

PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: There’s been quite a lot of leadership instability in the Health Department...we started off with one MEC, who was then replaced with another one after the 2014 elections, the same MEC came back, left earlier this year. We now have in theory the fourth MEC. If we look at the administrative leadership, since 2009, we’re probably now at the fifth or sixth person. And so, it’s very difficult when you have that level of instability to implement programs successfully.

MEC Gwen Ramokgopa has been vocal on the department’s challenges.

UPS NEWS24 CLIP: “SYSTEM IS STANDING”: And I’ve always said that the two major financial challenges the department has is the accruals that are inherited from the past as well as the high medico-legal costs...

This week, there’s hope the department’s furniture may be released from the sheriff’s warehouse after the provincial treasury intervened. And at last, Sipho may get the help he’s been waiting for.

OLOF JOUBERT, MEDICAL MALPRACTICE ATTORNEY: I can be glad to say that today we met with the Department of Treasury...and they said they are going to assist in the facilitation of the payment of these claims and it’s on its way. It’s on its way. We’ll be able to set up a trust and we can help young Makhoba.

PROMOS
15 secs
The revolving door at the top has left the Gauteng Health Department in a shambles.
PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: Insufficient planning, that would be putting it euphemistically...I think there’s been poor planning, there’s been insufficient attention paid to holding people accountable.

15 secs
Millions due in medical negligence payouts is slowly throttling the public healthcare system.
THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: A 4-year-old, for instance, in respect of who the court has awarded R20 million does not necessarily need that R20 million now.

10 secs
In arrears before the budget year even started, the Gauteng Department of Health is battling to settle massive negligence payouts. Can it claw its way out of this financial mess?

JESSIE MAKHOBA: I cannot cope, I sit and think of all the things I could be doing and I can’t now. What Sipho needs is his mother’s love, if it were up to me I would not be working but I have to. It was outstanding payouts to the Makhobas and families like them that saw the sheriff remove furniture and more from the Department. The order was obtained by medical malpractice attorney Olof Joubert. CLAIRE MAWISA: A lot of people want to know Olof, was it a publicity stunt to get the furniture seized or was it a legitimate way to get that money for your client? OLOF JOUBERT, MEDICAL MALPRACTICE ATTORNEY: We have attempted and have been reasonable in all aspects. There’s a major amount of money still outstanding in which they defaulted on other matters. This was not a publicity stunt at all. Makhoba shares a tiny RDP house with two grown daughters, and Sipho who needs constant supervision. When he was born, she needed an emergency caesarean but she was sent from one hospital to the next, made to wait for hours and was subjected to painful vacuum extraction -- all to no avail. JESSIE MAKHOBA: Around twelve they took me to the theatre for a c-section, but by then it was too late, the baby was injured. The court vindicated Makhoba’s claim, but the battle wasn’t over. LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: The Health Department’s core responsibility is to take care of its patients but what must happen if they are the ones that cause the damage? The department’s legal services chief director Thulani Mlambo says they’re not allowed to budget for negligence payouts as the law deems it wasteful expenditure. CLAIRE MAWISA: Currently how many medical negligence claims do you have? THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: We are sitting at over 2000 matters. CLAIRE MAWISA: What happened when the furniture was seized? THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: The Department has not met its obligations in terms of the court order. So that’s why the sheriff had to come, and firstly attach the furniture. And then if you fail again to pay, they remove the furniture. Mlambo didn’t want to show us the empty floors, but claimed it was business as usual inside. DA shadow MEC for health Jack Bloom was barred from paying an oversight visit. JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: I don’t know how the staff are managing to work without furniture. I was told they hid their laptops...so maybe they still got their cell phones. I mean you can’t go on like this. Wits Public Health Professor Laetitia Rispel, a former health department head, has warned of systemic problems for over a decade. PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: Insufficient planning, that would be putting it euphemistically… I think there’s been poor planning, there’s been insufficient attention paid to holding people accountable. Bloom asked for the numbers in the provincial legislature. JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: The problem is they start off the financial year which is in April with more than R4 billion of accruals. This is basically debts that they owe to to suppliers of the Department. PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: By the 15th of every month, each Government department has to submit a set of financials to the provincial treasury. So it’s not a sudden problem...they would have seen it coming, you know, since the beginning of the financial year. CLAIRE MAWISA: How did we get here? JACK BLOOM, DA SHADOW MEC FOR HEALTH: Every month for goods and services they have to pay about R600 million and they only pay out R450 million. So, every month it’s a R150 million that they’re not paying. I think the staff are doing what they can...but what do you do when you don’t have an ICU bed? Or the machinery isn’t working...so you don’t pay the suppliers, machinery is not working, a baby gets brain damaged, ends up in court and the settlement could be well over R30 million. Carte Blanche met Thembisa Nikelo two years ago. At 3, she went to hospital for burn wounds on her hands. Drips inserted into her feet became gangrenous and she had to have a double amputation to save her life. The court awarded her just over R20 million for future medical expenses and damages. Thembisa’s mother, Celina. CELINA NIKELO: After she got injured, I had doubts about her quality of life, but her life has changed. She’s doing well in school, she's very bright and loves school. She still needs to go for check-ups, especially for her legs; there isn’t a lot of physio, but it’s a matter of changing the prosthetics as she outgrows them. LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: The Department says the rising number of negligence claims is harming its ability to run its hospitals and clinics. In August, it asked the Constitutional Court to change the law in these cases. The court is yet to deliver judgement. THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: What we are saying is that a 4 year old, for instance, in respect of who the court has awarded R20 million does not necessarily need that R20 million now. So we are requesting the Constitutional Court to actually allow us some kind of a certificate that can be given to that particular person who would have been wronged, to actually go to any institution in the country so that they can get care as and when it is required. CLAIRE MAWISA: But then what about other things that are not within the scope of the Department...schools...24 hour care? THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: We would pay as and when that particular service is actually needed. WIHAN JOUBERT, ATTORNEY SPECIALISING IN MEDICAL LAW: The first year or the second year the department will experience some relief, but I’m afraid it will be compounded -- payments will not be made, new applications will be brought... Medical law attorney Wihan Joubert is studying the Constitutionality of capping and staggering pay-outs. The Health Minister tasked the South African Law Reform Commission to see how the pressure of payouts can be relieved. WIHAN JOUBERT, ATTORNEY SPECIALISING IN MEDICAL LAW: At the time of publishing my research I couldn’t find a national procedure or guideline within which complaints by patients are handled...prospective claimants walking through my door do so as a last resort. In other words, they initiated a complaint. The complaint was acknowledged and it was promised that a… an investigation process will follow. And then sometimes, up to a year or two goes by without any feedback...I’m confident that should the hospital be in a position to properly investigate and sort out complaints, the incidences will rapidly decline. It’s rich for the Department to plead poverty, says Morné Mostert of civil rights watchdog AfriForum. They did a private investigation into a 2015 tender for equipment at a large Gauteng hospital after receiving leaked documents. MORNÉ MOSTERT, AFRIFORUM: Company A tendered for 24.1 million. Company B tendered for just over 12.7 million. Company B was disqualified on one single point on the tender evaluation form… All the information was on an annexure to the tender documentation and the bid acquisition committee disregarded that. A middleman appeared to have been paid to make sure Company A, a multinational, gets the deal at double the price. Afriforum asked the police and foreign anti-corruption agencies to investigate the wasteful expenditure. The Department did not respond to our questions about the tender. LINK CLAIRE MAWISA: Whether corruption, or rampant negligence -- the spectre of bankruptcy is turning the screws on the Department to take action… PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: There’s been quite a lot of leadership instability in the Health Department...we started off with one MEC, who was then replaced with another one after the 2014 elections, the same MEC came back, left earlier this year. We now have in theory the fourth MEC. If we look at the administrative leadership, since 2009, we’re probably now at the fifth or sixth person. And so, it’s very difficult when you have that level of instability to implement programs successfully. MEC Gwen Ramokgopa has been vocal on the department’s challenges. UPS NEWS24 CLIP: “SYSTEM IS STANDING”: And I’ve always said that the two major financial challenges the department has is the accruals that are inherited from the past as well as the high medico-legal costs... This week, there’s hope the department’s furniture may be released from the sheriff’s warehouse after the provincial treasury intervened. And at last, Sipho may get the help he’s been waiting for. OLOF JOUBERT, MEDICAL MALPRACTICE ATTORNEY: I can be glad to say that today we met with the Department of Treasury...and they said they are going to assist in the facilitation of the payment of these claims and it’s on its way. It’s on its way. We’ll be able to set up a trust and we can help young Makhoba. PROMOS 15 secs The revolving door at the top has left the Gauteng Health Department in a shambles. PROF. LAETITIA RISPEL, WITS UNIVERSITY SCHOOL OF PUBLIC HEALTH: Insufficient planning, that would be putting it euphemistically...I think there’s been poor planning, there’s been insufficient attention paid to holding people accountable. 15 secs Millions due in medical negligence payouts is slowly throttling the public healthcare system. THULANI MLAMBO, CHIEF DIRECTOR: LEGAL SERVICES DIRECTOR, GAUTENG HEALTH DEPARTMENT: A 4-year-old, for instance, in respect of who the court has awarded R20 million does not necessarily need that R20 million now. 10 secs In arrears before the budget year even started, the Gauteng Department of Health is battling to settle massive negligence payouts. Can it claw its way out of this financial mess?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Having its furniture seized to settle a legal claim may be a particularly low point, but it follows on years of bankruptcy in management and administration.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Last week the Gauteng health department had its furniture and office equipment seized to pay for a medical negligence claim of about R6,2-million. About 400 computers, 50 printers, 400 desks, 600 chairs, 200 filing cabinets, 10 fridges, 10 microwaves and three lounge suites have gone into storage -- keep in mind the total haul may not be worth more than about half a million rand. Keep in mind that the Department itself is now responsible to pay for the storage. Think about the replacement cost and new opportunities for graft as new tenders are issued to kit out the offices. Think of the time lost as staff reportedly sit on floors and commute to offices in Pretoria to be able to work. The seizure came after action was brought by Pretoria attorney Oloff Joubert, acting on behalf of a child who suffered brain damage when she was born at the Pholosong Hospital in December 2009. Joubert has confidentially informed us that he intends bringing further sheriff's action because of other unsettled claims -- in the interest of the children left behind. Joubert says his sense is that medical services may have improved in recent years and there seem to be fewer cases coming in, but many of the cases now crippling the system financially date back five years and more. He argues for a system similar to the private sector where doctors have insurance for negligence claims -- since negligence payouts are not budgeted for. (Keep in mind the national backdrop -- the South African Law Reform Commission is working on ways to stop the bleeding of the fiscus through lawsuits -- some very controversial suggestions are being put forward). But what about outstanding debts to suppliers? In May health MEC Gwen Ramokgopa conceded that the current R40.2bn budget was inadequate to cover requirements, largely due to substantial debt burden consisting of money owed to suppliers. Outstanding payments to suppliers dating back to previous years totalled R4.2bn. Commitments to long-term contracts took up R2.95bn, while possible payments for medical negligence amounted to R3.78bn. In 2016, the health department’s legal fees amounted to R569m, pushed up by burgeoning negligence cases since 2009. The department also reported that a total of R860m meant for hospital infrastructure had been withheld from the National Treasury pending submission and approvals of plans by the department. Of the total budget, R23.8bn was earmarked for the wage bill and R16.3bn for goods and services, while an estimated R6bn was allocated to accruals, the MEC said. "This budget is effectively not available," Ramokgopa said, "which means we have not been able to afford services in the past years and the service providers carried the public health system at a huge cost." The National Treasury’s fourth-quarter provincial budgets and expenditure report for the 2016-17 financial year released in April showed that provincial health departments spent 63% of their health expenditure on salaries. A meagre 4.4% of the total health expenditure went to capital expenditure. In 2016, the DEPT owed R300 million to 509 companies (mostly small and struggling...but some also large and struggling) according to answers to the DA's questions in the Gauteng Legislature. As of the end of January 2016, owed R296 million to 509 companies. In January 2017 the DEPT said: ​As the Gauteng Department of Health we wish to inform that we are paying all our suppliers but not full amount. This is due to prioritising payment as per demands which we cannot accede to because they are higher than what we budget for. This is compounded by the fact that the Department services other provinces and countries (which payment thereof is not consistent and sufficient). We are monitoring closely the stock management over what is available and what is needed at the facilities. This is to ensure we always have enough funds to pay suppliers. It is important indicating that Medico-Legal claims dating back 2009/10 and 2011 take bulk of the Department's budget. We wish to confirm that an amount of R11 billion has been paid to suppliers in this financial year (2016/17) and this will continue until the end of March 2017. All the outstanding amount will be settled in the new financial year. We asked where the money is going and who benefits.
metadata.Summary: The Gauteng Health department, with a budget of R40.2 billion a year, has paid R1.017 billion in the 18 months from January 2015 to settle 185 medical negligence claims. But the department has more than R20 billion in claims pending against it. This is not something that is budgeted for and these claims could cripple a department already struggling to cope with staff shortages, lack of maintenance of buildings and machines and a high volume of patients. The department has asked the Constitutional Court change the law to allow it to pay medical negligence victims with installments or as and when they need medical attention. This request has failed before the courts in the past, but the department is making yet another last-ditch effort. The most medical negligence claims against the department originate in babies being brain-damaged at birth and by far the majority of claims originate at Chris Hani Baragwanath, where facilities are inadequate and understaffing endemic.
